en: Vimānavatthu: The Mansion of the Man,
Chapter on Well-Placed [Offerings]
9. The Mansion of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī “Adorned with polished earrings,
wearing garlands, and anointed with yellow sandalwood paste;”
“Raising your arms you weep;
why are you so distressed in the midst of the forest?
“I am made of gold, radiant...”
"A chariot-fender has been produced for me,
yet I cannot find a pair of wheels for it;
because of that suffering, I am giving up my life."
“Tell me, O auspicious young man, [whether it was] made of gold, made of jewels, made of red coral, or made of silver.”
“I shall set the wheel and yoke in motion for you.
That young brahmin replied to him:
“Both the moon and the sun are seen here.”
“My chariot is made of gold;
it shines with its wheels and yoke.
“You are a fool, young man!”
"You who desire that which is undesired—
I think you will die,
for you shall not obtain the moon and the sun."
“Going and coming are seen,
as is the color-element on both sides of the path;
but one who has passed away and died is not seen.”
“Who, indeed, is more foolish than one who weeps?
“You speak the truth, young man;
I alone am more foolish than one who weeps.”
Crying like a child in the moonlight,
he longs for the dead who have passed away.
Alas, while I am burning, he desires me as if I were already on fire!
Like a fire doused with a jar of water, by sprinkling it with water,
one should extinguish every dart of suffering.
Truly, the dart has been pulled out from me—
the sorrow residing in my heart— that which [pierced] me while I was overcome by grief.
I have dispelled the grief for my son.
My dart has been pulled out;
I have become cooled and attained Nibbāna.
“I do not grieve, nor do I weep,
O youth, having heard from you.
“Are you a deity, or are you a gandhabba?”
“Are you Sakka, the Giver of First Fruits? Or who are you, whose son are you?
How are we to know you?”
“Though you weep and though you wail,
having yourself cremated your son on the funeral pyre— I, for my part,
having performed wholesome deeds, [shall fare well].”

“Whether little or much, we did not see [any gift] being given by him in his own home; he has gone to the company of the Thirty-Three. “We did not see either little or much as he was giving alms in his own home;”
“Or by what kind of observance-duty have you gone to the world of the gods?
“I am afflicted, suffering, and ill.”
While I was in my own home, sick and afflicted,
I beheld the Buddha, free from passion, who had crossed over doubt—
the Well-Gone One of peerless wisdom.
With a joyful mind and a clear heart,
I joined my palms in reverence to the Tathāgata;
having performed that wholesome deed, I—
“He has gone to the company of the Thirty-three.
“It is wonderful, it is marvelous!
Such is the ripening of this act of joining the palms!”
“I too, with a joyful mind and a clear heart,
go this very day for refuge to the Buddha.
“Go this very day for refuge to the Buddha.”
With a mind full of confidence in the Dhamma and the Saṅgha,
likewise undertake the five precepts of training,
keeping them unbroken and flourishing.
Quickly abstain from taking life;
avoid what is not given in this world;
do not drink intoxicants, and do not speak falsehoods.
“Be content with your own wife. “You desire my welfare, O Yakkha;
you desire my benefit, O Devatā.”
"I shall do your bidding; you are my teacher.
Thus I go for refuge to the Buddha.
And the unsurpassed Dhamma,
and the Sangha of the God among Men—
I go to them for refuge.
I quickly abstain from taking life;
I avoid what is not given in the world;
I do not drink intoxicants, nor do I speak falsehoods.
“I am content with my own wife.
Thus ends the ninth *Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī-vimāna*.
